description: We're Mouloud and Yasmine, two final-year students. Mouloud is in Computer Science at Université de Sherbrooke, with three internships in full-stack development and applied AI, and research experience forecasting emergency calls across Québec.
summary: Since 2012 NASA has watched fires with two sensors. A record that joins MODIS (before 2012) and VIIRS (after) jumps in 2012, because VIIRS is sharper and records about twice as many fire detections. FireBridge measures that factor in the years when both sensors fly, puts the 2001–2011 record on the VIIRS scale, and shows a harmonized burning calendar for any area of Canada or Argentina, from 2001 to October 2026. The answer changes. In Argentina the naive record says detections rose 1.45×; on one scale they fell (0.68×). In Canada 4.23× becomes 2.01×, close to official area burned (1.92× official, 1.88× ours). One offline HTML file, no install, and it says "uncertain" where the data cannot tell.
details:
Try it: https://mouloud08.github.io/BlackCoffeeOnly-Nasa-Space-Apps/ · Code, data and the offline file (GitHub): https://github.com/Mouloud08/BlackCoffeeOnly-Nasa-Space-Apps · 30-second demo: https://mouloud08.github.io/BlackCoffeeOnly-Nasa-Space-Apps/demo.mp4

The problem

A long fire trend from NASA FIRMS joins MODIS (from 2000; our record starts in 2001) and VIIRS (from 2012, 375 m pixels, so it also sees small fires), a second, sharper pair of eyes flying alongside the first. The 2012 seam then looks like a rise in fire. Raw points exaggerate the gap: in the two FIRMS extracts the app embeds, VIIRS S-NPP has 1,686 points to MODIS's 418 (Terra + Aqua; La Rioja, August 2024) and 81,841 to 14,746 (Boreal Québec, June 2023). So we compare the sensors on one grid.

What it does, in 4 steps

  1. Count cell-days (a ~1 km square where a satellite saw fire that day) per month on 0.5° squares, the same grid for both sensors.
  2. Measure the jump where both fly (2012–2025): VIIRS ÷ MODIS = 2.10 over Canada, 2.13 over Argentina, measured for each selected area (small areas borrow it from a wider one).
  3. Bridge: MODIS months before 2012 × that ratio; VIIRS months unchanged. The record, 2001 to October 2026, reads on the scale of the sensor that continues.
  4. Test, and say when we cannot tell: overlap years predicted from each other; the trend re-run without its biggest year and with resampled years. Too small or too variable: the factor and "uncertain", no rise.

Try it first: three screens, two minutes

  1. The flip. Argentina, Record years map: click Raw, then Harmonized. Each square shows whether its busiest fire year came before or after 2012; on one scale, 223 places move to "before 2012", none the other way.
  2. The checks. Evidence, Canada: harmonized 1.88×, official area burned 1.92× (same years), records simply joined 3.96×. The verdict pills read "Correction A · reliable" and "Still up without 2023".
  3. Your own area. Calendar → click the map, Draw area, or the zone picker → Enter coordinates…: the calendar, the verdict and the checks recompute.

For the judges, in four paragraphs

Impact. When MODIS stops, every FIRMS time series becomes VIIRS-only; FireBridge gives the factor that puts the 2001–2011 archive on that scale, zone by zone, with a stated quality. The stakes: Canada reads 4.23× joined, 2.01× harmonized; in Argentina the sign flips. Built for analysts who draw fire trends from FIRMS and must judge whether a rise, or this month, is unusual for their area: one offline file, no account, no network, every number sourced.

Creativity. One question ("is the rise real, or is it the satellite?"), one switch that flips every view between the two answers, and a Record years map whose squares change colour when the records share one scale. The app refuses to print a trend the data cannot support, and already continues S-NPP outage months on NOAA-20 (NOAA-20 ÷ S-NPP = 1.01), the path the record takes after S-NPP. The next method step is already measured out of sample: a seasonal correction (see "What we would do next").

Validity. The correction is tested where both sensors fly; the trend against official area burned and without its biggest year (details below). One metrics module computes every figure; a self-check prints them all.

Relevance. Every requirement answered (table below), NASA FIRMS (the challenge's listed resource) for every detection, Argentina (the challenge author's country) and Canada, to October 2026.

How it answers each requirement of the challenge

Clicks from the first screen (Overview). Tabs: Overview, Calendar, Evidence, How it works, Method.

  • Harmonized MODIS + VIIRS. Default everywhere; the Raw | Harmonized switch (keys R / H) flips map, calendar and numbers. (clicks: 0 (1 to compare))
  • Burning calendar, months × years. Calendar tab: month rows, year columns 2001–2026, the 2012 seam labelled. (clicks: 1)
  • Region by map. Calendar → click a place (2° box), Draw area, or move / resize the box. Layers: Detections, Record years, Sensor effect, One month. (clicks: 2)
  • Region by coordinates. Zone picker → Enter coordinates… (clicks: 2 + typing)
  • Date range. Calendar → the date-range button ("2001 – Oct 2026"). (clicks: 2)
  • Downloads, including hotspot CSV. Download (top bar, every tab on desktop). This zone: series CSV, calendar SVG / PNG, map layer CSV. Real FIRMS hotspots: La Rioja · Aug 2024, Boreal Québec · Jun 2023 (original points, unchanged, with point count and size); Another area or period… gives the exact FIRMS request for any other area (the app holds monthly counts, not individual detections). (clicks: 2)
  • Accessible colour ramps. Ramps checked for colour blindness and grayscale; sensors told apart by shape (MODIS hollow, VIIRS filled); light and dark themes; keyboard; Glossary. (clicks: 0)
  • Current month vs historical median. Calendar → click a month: compared with the median of that month, 2003–2025; Anomaly mode; One month layer. October 2026, Argentina. (clicks: 2)

Validation

  • Why not simply use MODIS alone? For the single before/after figure, MODIS alone gives the same answer, by construction: the years before 2012 are multiplied by the ratio that links VIIRS to MODIS after 2012, so the ratio cancels. That equality validates nothing. The harmonized record gives what MODIS alone cannot: a month-by-month calendar and month ranks on the scale of the sensor that continues, so the record does not break when MODIS stops.
  • The correction itself. Each overlap year (2012–2025) predicted from the others: median error 3% in both countries. Trained on 2012–2018, the ratio predicts 2019–2025 within 7% (Canada) and 5% (Argentina); median monthly error 16% and 12%. Leaving one year out keeps the ratio within 2.07–2.12 (Canada) and 2.11–2.15 (Argentina).
  • The trend against an independent source (a check of the trend, not of the correction). Canada's National Forestry Database, independent of both sensors, mean year 2012–2024 against 2003–2011: official area burned 1.92×, harmonized 1.88×, records simply joined 3.96×.
  • Argentina: a consistency check, not a ground check. A satellite burned-area record with no sensor change in 2012 (Global Wildfire Information System, from NASA's MODIS MCD64A1 product) shows 0.78× as much area burned per year in 2012–2024 as in 2003–2011; on the same years our harmonized detections give 0.69× and the records simply joined 1.46×. Year by year, burned area ranks like the harmonized record (rank correlation 0.79) far more than like the joined one (0.32). That product is also MODIS-based: it supports reading the post-2012 rise as a sensor effect, but it is not an agency series like Canada's.
  • The trend without its biggest year. Canada 2.01×, still 1.62× without 2023 (90% resampled range 1.30–2.92); Argentina 0.68×, 0.62× without 2020 (0.57–0.82). Both robust.
  • False records from the seam? Share of 0.5° places whose busiest year is 2012 or later, against chance (2,000 reshuffles of the year labels). Canada: joined 84.1%, above chance (42.7%–76.3%); harmonized 73.7%, inside (44.7%–74.5%). Argentina: joined 70.0%, inside (42.2%–76.7%); harmonized 38.7%, below (41.9%–78.7%).
  • Knowing when to stop. Boreal Québec: 1.63× harmonized, but 0.67× without 2023 and a 90% range of 0.13–4.72. The app prints no rise there, only the correction factor (2.12) and the reason.

Limits we declare

  • Fire detections, not burned area.
  • Argentina has no ground-based check: its result rests on MODIS records (the detections, and a MODIS burned-area product that agrees with them). We assembled Argentina's official fire statistics (Programa Nacional de Estadística Forestal, 20 of the 22 years) and they cannot settle it: they add up what each province declares, with different provinces missing in different years, so their 2012–2024 ÷ 2003–2011 ratio moves from 0.75× to 1.37× when a single year is left out (0.85× with all years, 1.37× without 2003). On the one near-complete window (2012–2016 against 2009–2011) they show a rise, 1.34×, where our harmonized record shows 0.71×: three years against five, driven by one province. That series neither confirms nor refutes our result (node scripts/check_argentina_national.mjs).
  • One pooled ratio per zone leaves a seasonal residual (Canada: March 4.10 against 2.10), disclosed, not corrected in the app. We measured the correction (see "What we would do next").
  • Places with a local ratio above 4× (62 in Canada, 27 in Argentina) are not harmonized; cause not investigated.
  • 4.1% (Canada) and 5.5% (Argentina) of VIIRS cell-days fall where MODIS saw nothing that month: a ratio cannot put those back.
  • Quality thresholds are our heuristics, calibrated on Québec.
  • 2026 is partial (to October), outside yearly statistics, its last months provisional. As recorded in the FIRMS availability on 15 November 2026, the S-NPP near-real-time data end on 2 November 2026; the record continues on NOAA-20 (1.01 times S-NPP in both countries).
  • Two countries only.

What we would do next

  • First, a usable ground-based series for Argentina: the national statistics we assembled are too uneven (provinces missing by year); a check needs province-level series restricted to provinces that reported every year.
  • A seasonal correction, measured, not yet in the app. One VIIRS ÷ MODIS ratio per calendar month, pulled toward the single ratio when a month has few fires. Tested on years left out one at a time, it predicts VIIRS months better than today's single ratio: median monthly error 16.5% → 11.7% in Canada and 11.7% → 6.9% in Argentina, lower in 12 of 14 and 14 of 14 left-out years; Canada's worst calendar month goes from 1.95× off to 1.19×. The headline rises do not move (Canada 2.01×, Argentina 0.68×). It brings no clear gain in small zones, and an independent review of our prototype found what it still lacks: the month factors are not capped, so in a small area a month where MODIS saw very few fires can get a factor far above the app's 4× limit. It stays out of the app until that is fixed (node research/seasonal.mjs, report in research/SEASONAL.md; prototype in research/seasonal-app/).
  • Two ideas tested and set aside (node research/spatial.mjs, research/SPATIAL.md). Ratios that vary place by place did not help at the scale of a selected area (error of predicted VIIRS counts in 2° boxes, years left out one at a time: 15.5% → 15.2% in Canada, 9.9% → 9.7% in Argentina), so the app keeps one ratio per zone. Adding the small fires VIIRS sees where MODIS saw nothing helps a little (15.5% → 14.1%, 9.9% → 9.1%) but puts fire in months where MODIS recorded none (8.1% of Canada's 2003–2011 total): an assumption about the past, not a measurement, so it stays out.
  • Any country (FIRMS covers the world); hotspot points for any box and date; monthly updates carried through NOAA-20 and NOAA-21.

Tools, languages and software

JavaScript/JSX, React 18, esbuild (one self-contained HTML file, network blocked by its content security policy); Node.js scripts (FIRMS fetch, tiles, self-check); puppeteer-core, headless Chrome, axe-core; topojson-client, world-atlas; GitHub Pages; Visual Studio Code. AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) through Claude Code for coding, code review and search; ElevenLabs for the video voice.
